x.ASV: A Psalm of Asaph. The Mighty One, God, Jehovah, hath spoken, And called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof.
x.Darby: A Psalm. Of Asaph. God, Elohim-Jehovah, hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof.
x.KJV: A Psalm of Asaph. The mighty God, even the Lord, hath spoken, and called the earth from the rising of the sun unto the going down thereof.
x.YLT: A Psalm of Asaph. The God of gods--Jehovah--hath spoken, And He calleth to the earth From the rising of the sun unto its going in.

nt: Asaph is using a possessive form to express a superlative meaning. If a speaker of your language would not use a possessive form as a superlative, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The Supreme God] or [The God who is greater than all other gods]

Here, **the earth** represents the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting]

Asaph is referring to the entire earth by naming two extremes, the east, where **the sun** rises, and the west, where the sun sets. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people who live everywhere on earth]

x.ASV: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined forth.
x.Darby: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty,God hath shined forth.
x.KJV: Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God hath shined.
x.YLT: From Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shone.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **perfection** and **beauty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the perfectly beautiful place]

Asaph is speaking as if God had actually **shined forth** from Zion. He is using the image of light to represent God’s presence radiating out from Zion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God’s presence radiates out]

x.ASV: Our God cometh, and doth not keep silence: A fire devoureth before him, And it is very tempestuous round about him.
x.Darby: OurGod will come, and will not keep silence: fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him.
x.KJV: Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him.
x.YLT: Our God cometh, and is not silent, Fire before Him doth devour, And round about him it hath been very tempestuous.

nt: By **Our**, the psalmist means to include both himself and those he is addressing, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **silent**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and he is going to speak]

Asaph is using images from God’s appearance on Mount Sinai, where he made a covenant with the Israelites, to describe God’s approach to judge his people in light of that covenant on this occasion. [Exodus 19:16–18](../exo/19/16.md) describes how a great thunderstorm and a burning fire preceded Yahweh’s descent onto Mount Sinai. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. The UST models one way to do that.

Here, **to his face** represents “in front of him.” If you decide to retain this image in your translation, if it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [A fire devours in front of him]

Asaph is speaking as if this **fire** were actually devouring or eating what was in front of God. If you decide to retain this image in your translation, if it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A fire burns up everything in front of him]

The expression **it is stormed** is a passive verbal form. If you decide to retain this image in your translation, if your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [a great storm rages]

x.ASV: He calleth to the heavens above, And to the earth, that he may judge his people:
x.Darby: He will call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people:
x.KJV: He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people.
x.YLT: He doth call unto the heavens from above, And unto the earth, to judge His people.

nt: Asaph assumes that listeners will understand that he means that God **calls** the **heavens** and the **earth** to serve as witnesses of what the Israelites promised to do when they made a covenant with Yahweh. [Deuteronomy 4:26](../deu/04/26.md) and [Deuteronomy 30:19](../deu/30/19.md) describe how Moses called upon the heavens and the earth to serve as witnesses in this way. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He calls to the heavens above and to the earth as witnesses]

x.ASV: Gather my saints together unto me, Those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.
x.Darby: Gather unto me mygodly ones, those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice!
x.KJV: Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.
x.YLT: Gather ye to Me My saints, Making covenant with Me over a sacrifice.

nt: This verse is a direct quotation of God. The ULT indicates that by putting the verse inside quotation marks. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could also use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [He says, “Gather my faithful ones to me]

Asaph does not identify to whom God is giving this command. (God is not addressing the heavens and the earth. Their role is to serve as witnesses.) The focus is more on the results than on the agents. It may be more natural in your language to express this with a form other than a command form. Alternate translation: [Let my faithful ones be gathered to me]
The implied “you” in the imperative **Gather** is plural, so if you retain the command form, use its plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Asaph is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can use an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the ones who are faithful to me]

God is using **the cutters of my covenant** as a common expression of this culture to mean “those who made a covenant with me.” He is using the term “cut” because in some covenant ceremonies, the participants would cut up animals and then walk between the pieces. This was to indicate, “If I break this covenant, may I be destroyed in this same way.” It is not necessary to understand this background to covenant ceremonies in order to understand what God says in the rest of this psalm, so you do not have to use the term “cut” in your translation. You could simply say “make,” or you could use an expression from your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [those who made a covenant with me]

God is not using the phrase **by sacrifice** to refer to animals that were slaughtered and cut up when he made his covenant with the Israelites. (There is no description in the Bible of such a ceremony connected with that covenant.) He means that this covenant was sealed and was to be continually acknowledged by sacrificial worship, which is the main theme of this psalm. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that was sealed and was to be continually acknowledged by sacrificial worship]

x.ASV: And the heavens shall declare his righteousness; For God is judge himself. [Selah
x.Darby: And the heavens shall declare his righteousness; forGod executeth judgment himself. Selah.
x.KJV: And the heavens shall declare his righteousness: for God is judge himself. Selah.
x.YLT: And the heavens declare His righteousness, For God Himself is judge. Selah.

nt: Asaph is speaking of the **heavens** as if they were a living thing that could **declare** God’s righteousness. This conveys two ideas. In the immediate context, the heavens witness that God has kept his part of the covenant. In the broader biblical context, as in [19:1](../019/001.md) and [97:6](../097/006.md), the characteristics of the heavens display the righteous character of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the broader meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The heavens display his righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [that he is righteous]

Asaph is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though it could be omitted, in order to emphasize that the heavens declare that God is the supreme **judge** of everyone on earth. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the emphasis here. Alternate translation: [that it is God who is judge]
See how your translation team decided at [3:2](../003/002.md) to represent the term **Selah**.

x.ASV: Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify unto thee: I am God, even thy God.
x.Darby: Hear, my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify unto thee: I amGod, thyGod.
x.KJV: Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against thee: I am God, even thy God.
x.YLT: Hear, O My people, and I speak, O Israel, and I testify against thee, God, thy God am I.

nt: This verse begins a direct quotation of God that continues through verse 15. The ULT indicates that by putting these verses inside quotation marks. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could also use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [He says, “Hear, my people, and I will speak]

The pronouns **you** and **your** and the implied “you” in imperatives are singular here and through verse 15 because God is addressing his **people** as if they were a single individual. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [listen, Israel]

Here, **Israel** represents the nation that consisted of the descendants of Jacob, whom God renamed Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [you Israelites]

x.ASV: I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices; And thy burnt-offerings are continually before me.
x.Darby: I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices, or thy burnt-offerings, continually before me;
x.KJV: I will not reprove thee for thy sacrifices or thy burnt offerings, to have been continually before me.
x.YLT: Not for thy sacrifices do I reprove thee, Yea, thy burnt-offerings Are before Me continually.

nt: לֹ֣א עַל־זְ֭בָחֶי⁠ךָ אוֹכִיחֶ֑⁠ךָ וְ⁠עוֹלֹתֶ֖י⁠ךָ לְ⁠נֶגְדִּ֣⁠י תָמִֽיד

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Your burnt offerings are always before me, so I do not accuse you regarding your sacrifices]

x.ASV: I will take no bullock out of thy house, Nor he-goats out of thy folds.
x.Darby: I will take no bullock out of thy house, [nor] he-goats out of thy folds:
x.KJV: I will take no bullock out of thy house, nor he goats out of thy folds.
x.YLT: I take not from thy house a bullock, From thy folds he goats.

nt: Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not take a bull from your house, and I will not take goats from your folds] or [I will not take a bull from your house or goats from your folds]

God is not saying that he will not accept bulls or goats from the Israelites as sacrifices. This psalm as a whole is supportive of the sacrificial system. However, its emphasis is on offering sacrifices for the right reasons. They are not something that God needs; they are a way of living in relationship with God (as verses 14 and 15 especially emphasize). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I do not need to take a bull from your house or goats from your folds]

Here, a person’s **house** represents his “household” or “possessions.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from among your possessions]

Here and in v. 13, the psalmist is using a specific term that means male goats. If your language does not have a general term for goats but must specify whether a goat is male or female, use your term for male goats in these places.

x.ASV: For every beast of the forest is mine, And the cattle upon a thousand hills.
x.Darby: For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle upon a thousand hills;
x.KJV: For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills.
x.YLT: For Mine is every beast of the forest, The cattle on the hills of oxen.

nt: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Asaph is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle on a thousand hills are mine] or [every beast of the forest and the cattle on a thousand hills belong to me]

God is using the number **a thousand** in a way that was common in this culture to mean a very large, uncountable number, not a precise figure. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the cattle on every hill] or [all cattle everywhere]

x.ASV: I know all the birds of the mountains; And the wild beasts of the field are mine.
x.Darby: I know all the fowl of the mountains, and the roaming creatures of the field are mine:
x.KJV: I know all the fowls of the mountains: and the wild beasts of the field are mine.
x.YLT: I have known every fowl of the mountains, And the wild beast of the field is with Me.

nt: God is using the term **know** in a particular sense to mean that he owns **all the birds**. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I own]
In this context, the phrase **with me** expresses a relationship of possession. Alternate translation: [and the creature of the field is mine]

God is not referring to a specific **creature**. He means field creatures in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and every field creature is mine]

The term that the ULT translates as **creature** refers to a “moving thing,” and in this context, it probably means a “swarming thing” or insect. (In the previous verse, God described how large animals belonged to him, and in this verse, he makes the focus much smaller and thus even more comprehensive.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and even the insects in the fields are mine]

x.ASV: If I were hungry, I would not tell thee; For the world is mine, and the fulness thereof.
x.Darby: If I were hungry, I would not tell thee; for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof.
x.KJV: If I were hungry, I would not tell thee: for the world is mine, and the fulness thereof.
x.YLT: If I am hungry I tell not to thee, For Mine is the world and its fulness.

nt: אִם־אֶ֭רְעַב לֹא־אֹ֣מַר לָ֑⁠ךְ כִּי־לִ֥⁠י תֵ֝בֵ֗ל וּ⁠מְלֹאָֽ⁠הּ

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since the world and its fulness are mine, I would not tell you if I were hungry]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **fulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what fills it] or [and everything in it]

x.ASV: Will I eat the flesh of bulls, Or drink the blood of goats?
x.Darby: Should I eat the flesh of bulls, and drink the blood of goats?
x.KJV: Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?
x.YLT: Do I eat the flesh of bulls, And drink the blood of he-goats?

nt: הַֽ֭⁠אוֹכַל בְּשַׂ֣ר אַבִּירִ֑ים וְ⁠דַ֖ם עַתּוּדִ֣ים אֶשְׁתֶּֽה

God is using the question form to emphasize that what he is describing is certainly not true. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly do not eat the flesh of bulls, and I do not drink the blood of goats!]

x.ASV: Offer unto God the sacrifice of thanksgiving; And pay thy vows unto the Most High;
x.Darby: Offer untoGod thanksgiving, and perform thy vows unto the Most High;
x.KJV: Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High:
x.YLT: Sacrifice to God confession, And complete to the Most High thy vows.

nt: זְבַ֣ח לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים תּוֹדָ֑ה וְ⁠שַׁלֵּ֖ם לְ⁠עֶלְי֣וֹן נְדָרֶֽי⁠ךָ

God is speaking of himself in the third person because he is giving an authoritative command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [Sacrifice a thank offering to me, God, and pay your vows to me, the Most High]

x.ASV: And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.
x.Darby: And call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.
x.KJV: And call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me.
x.YLT: And call Me in a day of adversity, I deliver thee, and thou honourest Me.

nt: Asaph is using the term **day** to mean “time,” since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in any time of trouble]

x.ASV: But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, And that thou hast taken my covenant in thy mouth,
x.Darby: But unto the wickedGod saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant into thy mouth,
x.KJV: But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth?
x.YLT: And to the wicked hath God said: What to thee--to recount My statutes? That thou liftest up My covenant on thy mouth?

nt: Asaph is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **one**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can use an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But to every wicked person]

The pronouns **you** and **your** are singular here and through verse 21 because God is addressing a representative **wicked** individual. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
מַה־לְּ֭⁠ךָ לְ⁠סַפֵּ֣ר חֻקָּ֑⁠י וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֖א בְרִיתִ֣⁠י עֲלֵי־פִֽי⁠ךָ

God is using the question form to rebuke wicked people who speak as if they were loyal to his covenant but who disobey its commandments. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is not to you to recount my statutes, and you should not lift up my covenant onto your mouth!]
מַה־לְּ֭⁠ךָ לְ⁠סַפֵּ֣ר חֻקָּ֑⁠י וַ⁠תִּשָּׂ֖א בְרִיתִ֣⁠י עֲלֵי־פִֽי⁠ךָ

God is using **What to you** as a common expression of this culture to mean that the person he is addressing has no valid connection with what he describes next. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have no business recounting my statutes or lifting up my covenant onto your mouth!] or [It is not appropriate for you to recount my statutes or to lift up my covenant onto your mouth.]

God is speaking as if his **covenant** were an object that this wicked person could actually **lift up** and put on his **mouth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [or that you should say that you are loyal to my covenant]

x.ASV: Seeing that thou hatest instruction, And castest my words behind thee?
x.Darby: Seeing thou hast hated correction and hast cast my words behind thee?
x.KJV: Seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee.
x.YLT: Yea, thou hast hated instruction, And dost cast My words behind thee.

nt: God is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you have** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what faithful people are doing, as described in the previous part of this psalm, and what this wicked individual is doing. Alternate translation: [for your part, you hate]

God is speaking as if his **words** were objects that this wicked person could actually **cast behind** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you disregard my words]
God is using the term **words** to represent what he says by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what I say to you]

x.ASV: When thou sawest a thief, thou consentedst with him, And hast been partaker with adulterers.
x.Darby: When thou sawest a thief, thou didst take pleasure in him, and thy portion was with adulterers;
x.KJV: When thou sawest a thief, then thou consentedst with him, and hast been partaker with adulterers.
x.YLT: If thou hast seen a thief, Then thou art pleased with him, And with adulterers is thy portion.

x.ASV: Thou givest thy mouth to evil, And thy tongue frameth deceit.
x.Darby: Thou lettest thy mouth loose to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit;
x.KJV: Thou givest thy mouth to evil, and thy tongue frameth deceit.
x.YLT: Thy mouth thou hast sent forth with evil, And thy tongue joineth deceit together,

nt: God is using the term **send** in a specific sense to mean “release” or “set free,” as in [Deuteronomy 15:12](../deu/15/12.md). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You release your mouth in evil]

God is speaking of this wicked person’s **mouth** as if it were itself a person that the wicked one could **send** away or release. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You say evil things without restraint]

God is speaking of this wicked person’s **tongue** as if it were itself a person who could **frame** (form or put together) **deceit**, which God is speaking of as if it were an object that could be assembled. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you make up deceitful things to say]

x.ASV: Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; Thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.
x.Darby: Thou sittest [and] speakest against thy brother, thou revilest thine own mother's son:
x.KJV: Thou sittest and speakest against thy brother; thou slanderest thine own mother’s son.
x.YLT: Thou sittest, against thy brother thou speakest, Against a son of thy mother givest slander.

nt: God is using **You sit** as a common expression of this culture to indicate that the action he describes next, **you speak**, is something that this wicked person does deliberately and continuously. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You sit around speaking] or [You habitually speak]

The word that the ULT translates as **brother** is a general term that in various contexts can mean a full brother or a half-brother, a kinsman, or a fellow Israelite. The phrase **the son of your mother** explicitly describes a full brother. (It is characteristic of Hebrew poetry for the second part of a line to intensify and sharpen the first part of a line.) If your language has a general term for a relative that can include a brother, it would be appropriate to use it to translate **brother**. If not, if your language has a term for a half-brother (a son of the same father but not of the same mother), you might use that to translate **brother**, and you might use your term for a full brother (a son of the same mother and father) in the second part of the verse.

x.ASV: These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; Thou thoughtest that I was altogether such a one as thyself: But I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes.
x.Darby: These [things] hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether as thyself: [but] I will reprove thee, and set [them] in order before thine eyes.
x.KJV: These things hast thou done, and I kept silence; thou thoughtest that I was altogether such an one as thyself: but I will reprove thee, and set them in order before thine eyes.
x.YLT: These thou didst, and I kept silent, Thou hast thought that I am like thee, I reprove thee, and set in array before thine eyes.

nt: This could mean: (1) that God is referring to himself in the third person by the name he revealed to Moses in [Exodus 3:14](../exo/03/14.md). If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [You thought that I, the I AM, was like you in my being] or (2) that God is repeating forms of the verb “to be” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. Another way to translate the original text is, “You thought that being, I was like you.” Alternate translation: [You thought that surely I was like you]

This sentence indicates the result of the reason that the previous sentence describes. It may be helpful to use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Therefore, you thought the being of I AM was like you]

God is using the term **array**, which often describes armies forming battle lines, in a legal sense to mean that he will present evidence in a compelling order. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will marshal the evidence against you]
Here, **eyes** represent sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for you to see]

x.ASV: Now consider this, ye that forget God, Lest I tear you in pieces, and there be none to deliver:
x.Darby: Now consider this, ye that forgetGod, lest I tear in pieces, and there be no deliverer.
x.KJV: Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces, and there be none to deliver.
x.YLT: Understand this, I pray you, Ye who are forgetting God, Lest I tear, and there is no deliverer.

nt: The implied “you” in the imperative **Consider** is plural because God is addressing everyone who does not pay attention to his commandments, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

God is speaking of himself in the third person because he is giving an authoritative command. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [you who forget me, God] or [you who disregard me, God]

God is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the people he is addressing an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [Otherwise, I will tear you, and no one will be able to deliver you]

God is speaking as if he would actually **tear** wicked people into pieces the way a lion tears its victim apart. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I punish you severely]

x.ASV: Whoso offereth the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifieth me; And to him that ordereth his way aright Will I show the salvation of God.
x.Darby: Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me; and to him that ordereth [his] way will I shew the salvation ofGod.
x.KJV: Whoso offereth praise glorifieth me: and to him that ordereth his conversation aright will I shew the salvation of God.
x.YLT: He who is sacrificing praise honoureth Me, As to him who maketh a way, I cause him to look on the salvation of God!

nt: God is speaking as if the person he is describing were actually **placing** or preparing a **way** or path on which he would walk. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the one ordering his conduct rightly]

In this context, to **look upon** salvation means to “experience” it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make him experience the salvation of God]

God is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making an authoritative promise. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I will make him experience my salvation]
